title: Oil Traders Ignore Growing Threat to Persian Gulf Supply | OilPrice.com

Crude oil prices are down this week, extending a losing streak prompted by predictions of a supply glut. The ones doing the predictions are citing the rebound in export flows out of the Persian Gulf, but they seem to be forgetting something. These export flows were up in September and October. Now, they’re down. The war is not over, and neither is the risk to global oil supply.

One recent indication of that was the news that Chinese refiners, state-owned and independent, have ramped up their buying from abroad—and not only from the Middle East. Sinopec, for instance, has bought about 20 million barrels of crude since the start of this month from West Africa alone, for delivery next month. That is equivalent to all Chinese refiners’ West African oil purchases in a typical month.

Yet purchases from the Middle East are also on the rise, the report, by Bloomberg, said, suggesting export rates are indeed normalizing. Except the number of tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz has gone significantly higher as well. Just at the beginning of this week, three tankers were damaged after they struck mines, although the UK Maritime Trade Operations said three vessels were struck by unidentified projectiles. Mines and/or attacks on tankers have become a daily occurrence in the chokepoint—and daily traffic rates are down. Related: Iraq Refuses to Accept OPEC+ Assessment of its Production Capacity

Indeed, tanker traffic in Hormuz was already down in early October, from the September rebound. That was according to Kpler, which has turned into the go-to source of tanker traffic information for all major outlets. It was Kpler analysts who said that by October 8, the number of tankers traversing the Strait of Hormuz had fallen to the lowest in two months, meaning July, to some 10.1 million barrels daily. “That is back to its September average, but 74% of its pre-war level,” the analysts noted at the time.

This does not exactly match the glut story that some investment banks and the International Energy Agency are putting forward, and that has depressed prices and quite likely lulled oil traders into a false sense of security that all is back to normal in the Persian Gulf and a formal peace is only a matter of time—even as President Trump suggested to Fox News that the United States could restart its attacks on Iranian targets in 2027.

Meanwhile, Kpler has reported that after hitting a wartime high of over 20 million barrels daily in mid-October, tanker traffic in Hormuz began to decline, first to 16.03 million barrels daily towards the end of the month, falling further to 15.77 million barrels daily for the first week of November, and further still to 13.96 million barrels daily for the second week of the current month.

Reuters’ Clyde Russell cited Kpler’s numbers in his latest column, noting that since the start of November, attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf had reached 12 so far, after a total of 17 recorded for October. “It seems more than just a coincidence that export volumes from the Middle East are trending lower as attacks on vessels are trending higher,” Russell noted. It is, indeed, quite hard to see these developments as a coincidence, but it is interesting that oil traders appear to be ignoring the latest data, instead hanging on to the assumption that the September rebound was irreversible and the global oil market is about to tip into oversupply.

This is a risky assumption because, as suggested by President Trump, the war is not over. There is no ceasefire. Just because there are no reports of bombs raining on Iran and its Gulf neighbors, it does not mean things cannot change, often rather abruptly, as we have seen earlier this year. And this, in turn, means that oil flows out of the Persian Gulf could tighten further, showing the glut story for what it most likely is: a story about wishful thinking more than fact.

This, in turn, means that prices could move higher again, and this could take the peace-assuming traders by surprise—unless they are paying attention to other news besides reports about a glut, that is. For instance, Iraq is trying to take control of its northern fields from the Kurdistan autonomous government; India and China are importing record volumes of Russian oil, not Middle Eastern oil; and the Yemeni Houthis are not tired of attacking Saudi targets with a preference for energy industry sites.

The security situation in the Middle East is far from okay, and with it, the prospects of a well-supplied oil market remain uncertain. While the perception of ample supply right now may be keeping prices in check, there is no guarantee this perception cannot change under the weight of a less pleasant reality on the ground.
